archetype.name: Pocket Passer (rhythm thrower in a run-first offense)
archetype.definition: A non-running pocket quarterback whose 2026 job is to get the ball out fast on screens and short throws off a top-tier run game, with occasional shots that have so far landed.

report.headline: Spotless two-start efficiency built on screens, leads and soft defenses, not yet proven.
report.take:
Penix took over in Week 3 after Cooper Rush and Tua Tagovailoa each started once. In two starts he has been about as efficient as a quarterback can be: 10.64 yards per attempt (1st of 42), 0.438 EPA per dropback (4th) and a 73.3% completion rate (2nd). Both games were road wins by three scores. The question is how much of that is him and how much is the setting.

The setting explains a lot. Atlanta is a run-first team: it passes 10 points less than expected in neutral situations (30th) and runs the ball at the second-best EPA in the league. Penix has thrown only 22.5 times a game. A third of his attempts (15 of 45) were behind the line of scrimmage, and 69% were under 10 air yards. His intended air yards have dropped to 6.81, down from a 8.9 aDOT last year, and his aggressiveness has fallen from 14.9% to 2.22%. With a 2.4-second time to throw and the league's lowest pressure rate (4.4%), he has barely been touched. That reads as a deliberate redesign: quick, clean, low-risk throws behind a running game. It also shows up where he used to struggle. His bad-throw rate has fallen from 22.5% (59th of 65) to 4.4%, and his CPOE has gone from -3.6 to +5.3.

The caveats are sharp. The opponents were Green Bay and New Orleans, now 26th and 30th in defensive EPA. Of his 47 dropbacks, 18 came with a lead of nine or more, at a ridiculous 1.177 EPA per play. In one-score situations he was at -0.035, slightly below average. The deep numbers (2.522 EPA, 34.3 CPOE) come from four attempts, and one receiver, Drake London, has produced most of the value at 1.194 EPA on 16 targets. Two seasons of below-average accuracy don't disappear in 45 throws. The cleaner mechanics may be partly real, but the system is doing a lot of the work.

Where it heads: the structure is sustainable. The run game, the protection and the quick-game diet are real, and they protect him from his worst habits. What will fade is 10-plus yards per attempt and the deep-ball luck, especially once he plays a competent defense in a close game. A reasonable expectation is a good, low-volume starter in the 7.5-8.5 YPA range, not a top-five passer.

strengths.title: Accuracy rebuilt by quick-game design
strengths.body: His bad-throw rate fell from about 22% in each of his first two seasons to 4.4%, and his CPOE turned positive. The cause is mostly what he is being asked to do: shorter targets, lower aggressiveness and faster decisions are easier throws. The design is repeatable, so some of the gain should hold, though not all of it.

strengths.title: Clean pockets, almost no sacks
strengths.body: He has been pressured on 4.4% of dropbacks, the lowest rate in the league, and has yet to take a sack under pressure. That comes from a 2.4-second release and an offensive line ranked 4th in hit rate allowed. It is sturdier than most early splits because the scheme produces it, but it depends on the line staying intact.

strengths.title: Run game sets up everything
strengths.body: Atlanta's rushing offense ranks 2nd in EPA, which keeps him in manageable downs and turns play-action and under-center snaps into easy completions. His under-center EPA (0.509) is even better than his shotgun EPA. This is the most durable part of his profile.

concerns.title: Inflated by blowouts and bad defenses
concerns.body: His production with a lead of nine or more (1.177 EPA on 18 plays) dwarfs his one-score work (-0.035 on 29 plays). Both opponents now rank in the bottom seven defensively. This isn't a flaw in his game, but it means the headline efficiency hasn't been tested in a competitive game against a real defense.

concerns.title: Career accuracy says regression
concerns.body: He posted a CPOE of -4.4 in 2024 and -3.6 in 2025, ranking 52nd or worse both times. Two years of evidence outweigh 45 attempts. The safer read is that the scheme hides the issue rather than fixes it.

concerns.title: Low volume, narrow target tree
concerns.body: At 22.5 attempts a game in the league's fourth-most run-heavy offense, his yardage ceiling depends on efficiency rather than volume. London accounts for most of his value, while Dotson and Branch have been negative per target. If defenses take London away, there isn't an obvious second option.

trend.note: Two near-identical starts: 9.5 and then 10.6 passing EPA, both blowout wins, with aggressiveness falling to zero in Week 4. It's consistent so far, but the two-game sample came entirely against bottom-tier defenses.

nextGame.headline: A close game against a stingy short defense tests the new Penix
nextGame.body:
Baltimore is a middle-of-the-pack defense, 15th in EPA, with a profile that cuts against how Atlanta has used him. The Ravens rank 4th against short passes, which is where 69% of Penix's attempts have gone. They are much softer deep (19th, 0.532 EPA) and against the run (26th). The likeliest script is Atlanta leaning on its run game in a one-score game, which is exactly the setting where Penix's efficiency has been ordinary. The deep opening exists, but he has attempted only four such throws.

Availability cuts both ways. Left tackle Jake Matthews, a 100%-snap starter, left the Saints game with a groin injury and is questionable. Losing him would test the near-zero pressure rate that his whole profile rests on. On Baltimore's side, Trey Hendrickson is out, Marlon Humphrey is questionable with a calf injury, and the Ravens already rank 24th in sack rate, so the pass rush is thin. The bigger swing is Lamar Jackson, who is questionable with an ankle injury; his coach said Monday he didn't know Jackson's chances. Baltimore's offense ranks 2nd in pass EPA. With Jackson, Atlanta probably needs Penix to keep pace; without him, the game likely shrinks into a run-and-defend contest that suits Atlanta's 1st-ranked run defense.

keyMatchups.title: Quick game vs. top-4 short defense
keyMatchups.body: Baltimore allows -0.136 EPA on short passes, 4th in the league, while Penix has thrown 31 of 45 passes behind the line or under 10 yards. If the screens and quick outs stall, the offense has to push the ball further than it has wanted to.

keyMatchups.title: Atlanta run game vs. leaky front
keyMatchups.body: Atlanta's 2nd-ranked rushing offense meets a Baltimore run defense ranked 26th. That is good for Atlanta's chances to win but caps Penix's passing volume, and it keeps play-action and under-center looks open.

keyMatchups.title: Left tackle vs. depleted rush
keyMatchups.body: Penix has done his best work to the left (0.666 EPA on 27 attempts), and Matthews' groin puts that side in doubt. Hendrickson's absence and Baltimore's 24th-ranked sack rate soften the blow.

nextGame.watch: Whether Atlanta keeps Penix in the quick game in a one-score second half or trusts him to attack Baltimore's 19th-ranked deep defense, and whether Matthews is protecting his blind side.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the structure to hold and the efficiency to come down. The run game, quick release and low pressure rate are scheme and personnel, so his sack and turnover rates should stay good. His yards per attempt should settle well below 10, toward the 7.2-7.4 range he posted in his first two seasons plus a modest boost from the cleaner design. Volume stays modest in an offense this run-heavy, so his passing yards will run below what his efficiency suggests.

The things most likely to regress are the deep-ball results (four attempts) and the blowout-driven EPA. The thing that could prove real is the accuracy gain. If his bad-throw rate stays in single digits against better defenses, that would be a genuine change from his first two years rather than a product of easy throws.
swingFactors: Jake Matthews' groin and the health of the offensive line
Whether the offense expands his aggressiveness in close games
Drake London's availability and target share

bets.reason: Atlanta's 2nd-ranked rushing offense faces Baltimore's 26th-ranked run defense, and Atlanta's 1st-ranked run defense limits the Ravens' ground game. Jackson's ankle adds downside for Baltimore. The edge grows if he is ruled out, though the line would move.

Atlanta's two overs (59 and 69 total points) came against the 26th- and 30th-ranked defenses. Atlanta passes 10 points less than expected and has the 8th-ranked defense. A run-heavy, one-score game projects lower, especially if Jackson sits.
Baltimore ranks 4th against short passes, his main diet. A close game should keep Atlanta running against a weak Ravens front, and he has averaged only 22.5 attempts even in blowouts.
Baltimore allows 1.25 QB TDs per game (5th fewest). Penix's red-zone passing has been shaky (2 of 6), and Atlanta will likely lean on the run near the goal line.

confidence.note: Two starts, 45 attempts, both blowouts against bottom-seven defenses, set against a contrary two-year career profile.
